newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian police in pre-election war crime clean-up.
newsitem.headline: Serbian police in pre-election war crime clean-up.

text.p: The arrest of a war crimes suspect in Yugoslavia this week showed authorities were trying to distance themselves from wartime atrocities before federal elections in November, political analysts said on Thursday.

Montenegrin police, ending three years of silence about a well-documented crime, said they had arrested a man linked to the abduction and massacre of Moslem passengers on a train travelling through former Yugoslavia in 1993.
Political analysts said the highly-publicised arrest was part of a purge of those with links to the war and notorious "ethnic cleansing" operations as November 3 elections drew near.
"The primary goal is to distance the authorities from the war and atrocities in particular," said Dejan Anastasijevic of the independent weekly Vreme.

After a devastating war that turned hundreds of thousands of Serbs into refugees, Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic was keen to wipe the political slate clean of war-related issues before the federal elections.
Hardline nationalists and war crimes suspects now represent a political "burden" and Milosevic wants to consolidate his rule now that the war is over, Anastasijevic said.
Milosevic was also under continuing international pressure to hand over suspects indicted by the U.N. war crimes tribunal in The Hague.
But diplomats and analysts said Belgrade had yet to go after any "big fish" responsible for war crimes and appeared to be singling out lower ranking figures.
Media said Nebojsa Ranisavljevic, 32, admitted to organising the abduction of Moslems from the train running between Serbia and Montenegro, which now comprise rump Yugoslavia.

A group of Serb paramilitaries stopped the Belgrade-Bar train on February 27, 1993 in Strpci, a small Serb-held town located inside a 20-km (12-mile) stretch of Bosnia through which trains must pass due to rugged mountain terrain.
They seized 21 passengers, all but two of them Moslems and all citizens of Serbia. Their fate was unknown till now despite promises of speedy investigation by the authorities.
Police said Ranisavljevic was a paramilitary in a group under the command of Milan Lukic that terrorised eastern Bosnia
The passengers were killed by Lukic and Boban Indjic, for whom an arrest warrant was also issued, and their bodies thrown into the Drina river, the police quoted Ranisavljevic saying.

The lack of progress in the investigation raised tensions in the mainly-Moslem area especially after Lukic was inexplicably released from a prison in Serbia in 1993 where he spent several months for unlawful possesion of arms.
Lukic lives openly in the eastern Bosnian town of Visegrad, where he owns a cafe, and there was no sign Belgrade was pushing for his arrest.
Bosnian Serb military sources say the Moslems were shot to provoke unrest in Serbia's mainly-Moslem area of Sandzak and draw Yugoslavia openly into the Bosnian conflict.
The arrest follows a series of revealing stories in the pro-government Belgrade press about war crimes committed by Serbs during fighting in Croatia and Bosnia.
Until this year, state media had ignored or denied well-publicised atrocities that prompted international outrage.

The newspaper accounts have tended to pin the blame for atrocities on paramilitaries while protecting the name of rank and file members of the Yugoslav army, which backed Serb rebellions in Croatia and Bosnia.
Ten days ago, Serbian media with close ties to the authorities confirmed for the first time that Serbs committed atrocities in the Croatian town of Vukovar in 1991.
